title: TOG — Math Puzzle Game Built with AI
summary: Grid-based math puzzle game in GameMaker Studio 2 for GAME 3720 — I specified features for AI coding tools, then tested and fixed the results in-game, delivering the arithmetic evaluator, conditional walls, lobby progression, menus, dialogue and graph camera across 125 of 262 commits in a 6-person team

data.text: TOG is a grid-based math puzzle game built in GameMaker Studio 2 for GAME 3720. Players push number, operator and variable blocks into equation slots, and the resulting curve is plotted on an in-game graph. A correct curve carries a key out of the graph, and keys open doors that lead back to a lobby hub. The project ran from June 1 to August 2, 2026, with 262 commits from 6 people. I created and owned the repository, managed merges into main, and made 125 of the commits.

I didn't write my part of the code by hand. I worked with AI coding tools, including OpenAI's Codex, and my job was the rest of the loop: deciding what each feature should do, describing it precisely, running it in the game, finding what broke, and sending it back with a concrete bug report until it behaved correctly. This post covers the features I delivered that way and what I learned about working like this in GameMaker.

Teammates built the rest. DrLemonade did the original movement and block pushing, the undo stack, multi-block chain pushing, the quadratic equation parser, and the Conway's Game of Life river animation that floods the graph. Others made the art, sound assets, player sprites, options UI and tutorial hints.

items.content: First playable prototype: the initial linear graph with point checks and the key and door system, the first version of the game loop, which the rest of the project grew out of.

Arithmetic tool row: I designed a mechanic where the player lines up blocks like 3*2+1 and the result rewrites the number block on the other side of the equals sign, with a flash and a sound. I asked for a proper expression evaluator rather than a string hack: operator precedence, parentheses, unary minus, decimals, and a clean fail state for malformed input. The result was a small recursive descent parser, eval.gml.

Conditional walls: walls carrying an inequality (< <= > >= == !=) that only let through number blocks satisfying it. They turn green or red with a sound on each attempt. This feature took the most test-and-fix rounds of anything I owned (see below).

Doors, lobby and progression: ranked doors that open as levels are cleared, stay locked until the tutorials are done, and play a lock animation. Finished levels can't be re-entered, the game returns you to where you left the lobby, and the final puzzle pieces appear once every level is finished. Lining them up fades into the epilogue.

Menus and screens: the title, pause and level-select modes, with the level-select grid navigable by mouse or keyboard, plus the credits screen and return buttons. Teammates later restyled the buttons and added the options panel and pause guide.

Dialogue and story: in-level dialogue that triggers on a timer, when the player walks into it, or after a puzzle is solved, and can react to lobby state. I also set up the prologue and epilogue scenes.

Graph grid and camera: the coordinate grid, snapping the graph to the room grid, and an auto-zoom that fits the view to the curve and eases in. I also connected the graph to the equation slots and keys, added coordinate labels on keys, cleared the plot for empty or invalid equations, and timed the river sounds to its phases.
Equation history: a panel listing the last 5 unique valid attempts as readable y = ax² + bx + c, with the correct one flagged. The equation slot locks once the answer is right.

Controls and game feel: held-key repeat for movement and undo, arrow keys, shift-to-pull (only when a block is directly next to the player), input blocked during menus, dialogue and animations, and sound effects on every player action. I also did the visual pass: glow and bevel on equation slots, shadows, block text colors for each state, moving the art from 32px to 64px, tile setup, decorations, and building level 1.

The spec is the work: results depended on how exactly I described behavior. "Add a wall that checks numbers" gets something that compiles. "A wall of any length, horizontal or vertical, that blocks a number block if its value fails the condition, checked against every wall the block overlaps, green on pass and red on fail" gets something close to right. Writing out edge cases before asking saved more time than anything else.

Testing is where the bugs show up: AI output usually handled the case I described and missed the ones I didn't. The conditional walls went through several rounds in the commit history: logic changes, then a vertical-wall bug, then walls overlapping each other. Each one surfaced only by playing through levels, and each fix started with me pinning down exactly which push, from which direction, broke it.

Interactions are the hard part: in a puzzle game, one push can go through a wall check, change a tool value, re-evaluate an equation, re-plot the graph and release a key. AI handles each feature well in isolation, but it doesn't see the whole game, so I had to keep that picture in my head and describe how the new feature should fit into it.

Knowing the engine still matters: GML is less common than JavaScript or Python, and GameMaker's room, instance and layer model shapes what works. Understanding how GameMaker runs objects and events is what let me tell a real bug apart from code that simply didn't fit the engine.

Git still has to be managed by hand: with six people and AI-generated changes landing in shared GameMaker project files, I kept main working by merging often and cleaning up conflicts myself. AI speeds up writing code, but it doesn't coordinate a team.

data.text: AI-assisted development (Codex), writing feature specs, playtesting and bug reproduction, GameMaker Studio 2 and GML, puzzle and progression design, UI and menu design, level setup, git repository ownership and merge management
